title: Dead Silence
full_review:
Ventriloquist's dummies and horror movies just seem to go together, but the usual scares don't materialize in the mechanical "Dead Silence" (Universal).

When wife Lisa (Laura Regan) is murdered, Jamie Ashen (Ryan Kwanten) returns to his hometown of Raven Fair to investigate. Homicide detective Jim Lipton (Donnie Wahlberg) tails Jamie, his prime suspect, who has taken along a key piece of evidence -- the doll that showed up on his doorstep right before the crime.

Local lore tells of a female ventriloquist named Mary Shaw (Judith Roberts), and it's her revenge that Jamie must confront after learning from his estranged, wheelchair-bound father Edward (Bob Gunton) that the Ashens have a history with Shaw and her collection of dolls.

Director James Wan teases a bit of mystery out of an ordinary plot, relying on auditory effects such as disembodied voices and the requisite amounts of fog, rain and lightning. But the film proves long on buildup and short on genuine frights.

Measured against today's horror standards, the movie has a low gore quotient. There are three murders and shots of tongueless cadavers, yet it's relatively free of mayhem, with most of the violence implied or off-screen.

The legend behind "Dead Silence" says that screaming will bring certain death. Given the dearth of goose-bump moments here, viewers needn't worry.

The film contains some crass language, violence, bloody images and dead bodies. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
